Title: A C–H Arylation‐Based Enantioselective Synthesis of Planar Chiral Cyclophanes
Text:

Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202500653 (1 of 8)
Asymmetric Catalysis
A C–H Arylation-Based Enantioselective Synthesis of Planar Chiral
Cyclophanes
Soohee Huh, Elvira Linne, Lilian Estaque, Grégory Pieters, Michael Devereux, and
Olivier Baudoin*
Abstract: Despite the growing importance of planar
chiral macrocyclophanes owing to their unique proper-
ties in different areas of chemistry, methods that are
effective in controlling their planar chirality are re-
stricted to certain molecular scaffolds. Herein, we report
the first Pd(0)-catalyzed enantioselective intermolecular
CH arylation that induces planar chirality by installing
bulky aryl groups through dynamic kinetic resolution
(DKR). A computer-assisted approach allowed a fine-
tuning of the structure of the employed chiral bifunc-
tional phosphine-carboxylate ligands to achieve high
enantioselectivities. A range of planar chiral macro-
cyclophanes were successfully synthesized from config-
urationally labile macrocyclic precursors via CH aryla-
tion
with
various
perfluoroarenes.
Mechanistic
investigations indicated that the reaction proceeds via
reversible oxidative addition and enantiodetermining
CH activation. Selected macrocyclophane products
showed interesting photophysical and chiroptical prop-
erties, which depended on both the nature of the ansa
chains and the aromatic moieties.
Introduction
Cyclophanes are a subfamily of macrocycles consisting of at
least one aromatic ring and ansa chain, which possess unique
three-dimensional structures and properties. Stable planar
chirality may arise from the restricted bond rotation of the
aromatic
ring(s),
if
suitable
ansa
chain
lengths
are
employed.[1] They display a wide range of applications in
fields such as host–guest chemistry, catalysis, drug discovery
and organic optoelectronics.[2] Perfluorinated arenes have
also garnered significant attention in recent years due to
their unique properties in pharmaceutical and material
sciences[3] and their excellent reactivity as CH activation
precursors.[4] The combination of these two classes of
compounds would therefore lead to potentially interesting
novel molecules whose intrinsic properties are unknown.
However, to the best of our knowledge, catalytic enantiose-
lective CH arylation methods for the synthesis of planar-
chiral perfluorinated cyclophanes have remained elusive.
Recently, elegant catalytic methods have been disclosed
for the enantioselective synthesis of planar-chiral cyclo-
phanes,
which
can
be
divided
into
four
different
approaches:[5] enantioselective construction of one aromatic
ring,[6] enantioselective macrocyclization,[7] desymmetriza-
tion of prochiral precursors[8] and dynamic kinetic resolution
(DKR) of conformationally labile substrates.[9] DKR is a
particularly attractive strategy to induce planar chirality in a
late-stage manner,[5c] and has been first employed by Shibata
through enantioselective Sonogashira coupling.[9a]
In the past decade, CH bond functionalization has
emerged as a powerful step-economical tool for the syn-
thesis of complex molecules and has proven to be suitable
for the control of diverse stereogenic units.[10] In this context,
Zhao and co-workers recently reported a DKR-based
enantioselective PdII-catalyzed CH olefination of macro-
cyclophanes
using
a
bidentate
directing
group
(DG)
strategy.[9d,g] Although this method allowed the synthesis of
planar chiral cyclophanes in good yields and enantioselectiv-
ities, the DG remains in the cyclophane product and
requires two additional steps for its introduction and
removal. A direct access to planar chiral macrocyclophanes
without the installment of a DG is highly desirable to
improve the preparation of these important chiral mole-
cules. Enantioselective Pd(0)-catalyzed CH activation has
proven
as
a
powerful
tool
to
build
diverse
chiral
molecules.[11] However, the control of planar chirality has
remained confined to ferrocenes and other metallocenes,[12]
probably due to the conformational flexibility of macro-
cyclophanes, which makes enantiocontrol more challenging
compared to more rigid systems. Inspired by the work of
Shibata,[9a] we hypothesized that a conformationally labile
macrocyclic aryl bromide 1 could undergo enantioselective
CH arylation via the DKR process illustrated in Scheme 1.
After CH arylation with an appropriate (hetero)arene in
the presence of a suitable chiral catalyst, the corresponding
product 2 would bear a larger (hetero)aryl ring which cannot
rotate inside the ansa chain and would therefore possess
planar chirality. Herein, we report the successful develop-
ment of an efficient asymmetric CH arylation method that
allows the synthesis of configurationally stable fluorinated
macrocyclophanes from configurationally labile precursors
through DKR in a single step. This allows construction of

Results and Discussion
To probe the feasibility of this DKR strategy, cyclophane
1a1
was
chosen
as
a
model
substrate
(Figure 1),
the
configurational lability of which was probed by
1H NMR
and compared with the resulting product 2a1-I. Indeed, the
most downfield methylene protons appeared as a triplet in
1a1 and a multiplet in 2a1-I, suggesting the configurational
lability of 1a1 and configurational stability of 2a1-I at room
temperature (see the Supporting Information, Figure S1). In
addition, the DFT-optimized geometry of 1a1 (Scheme 1b,
left) indicates that the short bond length of Cb–Br renders
the rotation of the aromatic ring possible through the ansa
chain, despite the presence of the bulky benzene ring. To
control planar chirality in this challenging Pd(0)-catalyzed
CH arylation, we turned to our bifunctional phosphine-
carboxylate ligands (Scheme 1b, right). Indeed, these versa-
tile
ligands
were
shown
to
provide
highly
organized
transition
states
and
high
enantioselectivities
in
CH
arylations leading to aromatic molecules with central,[13a–c]
inherent,[13d] and helical chirality,[13e] and we surmised that
they could be also suitable to generate complex planar chiral
systems. The first attempts with previously synthesized
ligands L1-L3 were promising (Figure 1), and indicated that
bulkier R substituents exert a beneficial effect on the
enantioselectivity (see Table S1 for more details). Motivated
by these findings, and considering CH activation as the
enantiodetermining
step
(see
below),
we
conducted
a
preliminary geometry optimization of the CH activation
transition state[13e] to get more structural insights and a
blueprint for the ligand design (Figure 2). In the optimized
geometry using t-Bu-substituted ligand L3, a close distance
between the phenyl moiety of the cyclophane substrate and
one t-Bu substituent of the ligand was observed. We
assumed that this close contact might rigidify the structural
environment, leading to a differentiation of diastereomeric
transition
states
(ΔΔG‡),
either
via
attractive
London
dispersion[14,15] or steric repulsion.[16] Starting from this
observation, we envisaged that a higher stretch of the ligand
toward the phenyl moiety of the substrate might lead to
higher enantioselectivities. In order to generate a library of
ligands bearing substituents of varying sizes, we synthesized
new bifunctional ligands including group-14 atoms with
bigger atomic radii (Si and Ge) in the substituent to estimate
their catalytic performance (L4-L8). Gratifyingly, when Si
and Ge substituents were introduced, enhanced enantiomer-
ic ratios were observed (L4-L11), with optimal enantioselec-
tivities for triethylsilyl and triethylgermyl groups (L6, L7).
With L9-L11 that contain a H8-binaphthyl core, a similar
trend was observed albeit in lower enantioselectivities.
Ligands featuring different substitution patterns and/or
different electronic properties showed no positive effect on
the observed e.r. values (L12-L15). We then performed
control experiments with monofunctional ligands L16 and L17
lacking the carboxylic acid moiety and external bases.[13a,b]
Interestingly, whereas no reaction was observed when a
carboxylate base (CsOPiv) was employed, CH arylation
occurred with cesium carbonate, albeit in lower yields and
much
lower
enantioselectivities.
This
implies
that
the
bidentate mode is not the only possible CH activation
mode despite its general superiority in this and previous
transformations.[13] In addition, increasing the amount of
carbonate to 2.5 equiv. instead of 1.5 equiv. when employing
ligand L6 led to a reduced e.r. value of 88:12 (Table S4).
Moreover, when identical reaction conditions were used
with deuterated perfluoroarene d-I, a significant degree of
D/H exchange was observed in the unreacted perfluoroar-
ene. These results indicate that a less selective carbonate-
mediated deprotonation of the fluoroarene competes with
the carboxylate-mediated CH activation process. Indeed,
CH arylation with perfluoroarenes was shown to proceed

Using
these
conditions,

the

synthesis of planar chiral macrocycles (Scheme 2). The

the
e.r.
being
observed,
and
other
products
behaved
similarly. Ligands L3-L4 bearing smaller t-Bu and TMS

on
the
aryl
substituent
of
reactant
1
without
significantly affecting the yield and enantioselectivity (2a1-I-
2b2-I). In addition, different substitution patterns on this
ring gave the desired products in moderate to good yields
with high levels of enantioselectivities (2b3-I, 2b4-I). The
current reaction was readily applicable to substrates bearing
an extended π-system, such as a naphthyl ring (2b5-I), as
well as various heteroarenes (2b6-I-2b8-I, 2a3-I). To our
delight, product 2a4-I bearing a phenylacetylene substituent
could be also obtained, albeit in decreased enantioselectiv-
ity. Moreover, a saturated N-heterocycle (2b9-I) was com-
patible with this approach, but a lower yield and enantiose-
lectivity were observed due to decomposition of the starting
material. Our protocol was also applicable to other perfluor-
oarenes such as pentafluorobenzene (2b10-II), 2,3,5,6-tetra-
fluorotoluene (2b10-III) and 2,3,5,6-tetrafluoropyridine (2a5-
IV) in high enantioselectivities, although lower yields were
obtained with III.

Unfortunately, we were not able to ascribe the absolute
configurations of the macrocyclophane products in this study
by X-ray diffraction analysis, due to their reluctance to
crystallize. However, the simulation of the ECD spectra of
the two enantiomers of compound 4h-I and their compar-
ison with the experimental ECD spectrum allowed to
ascribe its absolute configuration as (Rp) with confidence
(Figures S22–25), and the other absolute configurations
were ascribed by analogy.
A
simplified
mechanistic
proposal
is
depicted
in
Scheme 4. In light of numerous reports postulating the
oxidative addition (OA) of Pd(0) to Ar–X as an irreversible
process due to its exergonic nature, OA was initially
presumed to be the enantiodetermining step (hypothesis
1).[18,19] This initial assumption seemed reasonable consider-
ing the massive size of the ligand datively bound to Pd,
rendering the rotation of the aryl ring unfeasible in the OA
complex. On the other hand, recent reports showed that
reversible oxidative addition occurs in a number of catalytic
processes such as cross-coupling and carbohalogenation.[20]
However, experimental proofs of this reversibility revolve
around the mere observation of the regenerated aryl halide
from the OA complex,[21] and proving reversibility in
reactions that do not include halogen atoms in the product is
difficult. In fact, our attempts to isolate an OA complex to
probe reversibility to the aryl bromide precursor failed.

Instead, a series of reactions that proceed through the same
oxidative addition intermediates were designed. If the OA
step
is
irreversible
and
enantiodetermining,
the
same
enantioselectivities should be observed regardless of which
perfluoroarene is employed. Two different substrates 1a1
and 1a5 were thus reacted with different perfluoroarenes (I–
V) and in both cases stark differences in enantioselectivities
were observed (Scheme 5a), indicating that CH activation
is the enantiodetermining step (hypothesis 2). In search of
another corroborating evidence, the reactions of 3i and 1b10
and deuterated perfluoroarene d-I were performed to see a
potential change in enantioselectivity (Scheme 5b). Indeed,
a significantly increased e.r. was observed with d-I in both
cases. These experiments further indicate that CH activa-
tion is the enantiodetermining step.[22] We are not aware of
similar observations of such inverse product isotope effects
(e.r.H/e.r.D <1) in CH activation reactions. This effect is
particularly interesting, as it potentially furnishes a new
approach to increase enantioselectivity in such reactions by
employing a deuterated reagent.
Considering the increasing interest for chiroptical prop-
erties of chiral macrocyclophanes,[23,9g] the photophysical
(UV/Vis and fluorescence spectroscopies) and chiroptical
(ECD and CPL spectroscopies) properties of selected
macrocyclophane products were studied (toluene, c=10–5
M). Among these, two involve one non-symmetrical donor-
acceptor chromophore (2a1-I, 2a3-I), three contain one
symmetrical donor-acceptor chromophore (4a-I, 4b-I and
4d-I), and five possess two aromatic moieties bridged by
ansa linkers (4e~i-I). All cyclophanes displayed rather
intense UV bands (corresponding to the S0!S1 transition)
with absorption maxima and extinction coefficients ranging
from 326 to 365 nm and 5,094 to 15,573 L.mol–1.cm–1,
respectively. Moreover, all compounds except 4h-I and 4i-I
exhibited a fairly good fluorescence with photoluminescence
quantum yield (PLQY) values ranging from 0.15 to 0.41
and, in all cases, significant Stokes shifts ranging from
4,669 cm–1 (2a3-I) to 9,028 cm–1 (4g-I). Interestingly, whereas
4g-I, 4h-I, and 4i-I possess the same benzene units, the first
two compounds involving O4C12Ph and O4C10Ph ansa chains,
respectively, showed significantly higher Stokes shifts (9,028
and 8,980 cm–1) compared to 4i-I (7,161 cm–1). This may
suggest a potentially important impact of the ansa chain
nature on the interaction between the two aromatic moieties
or with the aromatic solvent in the excited states. To further
investigate this aspect, ECD and CPL spectroscopies were
employed. For all compounds, rather low absorption dis-
symmetry factor (gabs) values for the S0!S1 transition were
measured, ranging from 2.4×10–6 to 4.6×10–4 depending on
the nature of the ansa chain and aromatic units involved. It
is worth noting that for some compounds, rather large
differences between the gabs and emission dissymmetry
factor glum values were measured. This is likely due to large
geometry differences between the ground and excited states
linked to the relative flexibility of this type of cyclophanes.
The largest differences observed involve 4g-I, 4h-I (Fig-
ure 3) and 4i-I, compounds for which significant differences
in terms of Stokes shifts were also noticed. Indeed, while the
gabs values of the ECD band centered at ca. 330 nm are close
to 4×10–4 for all three compounds, the glum values of 4g-I and
4h-I are largely superior, reaching 1.6×10–3 and 2.3×10–3,
respectively, whereas for 4i-I the glum value (4.2×10–4) is
rather similar to the gabs (4.6×10–4). These results once again
suggest a potential interaction between the two aromatic
moieties or the aromatic solvent in the case of 4g-I and 4i-I
at the excited states, which will be the subject of future
investigations.
Conclusion
The first Pd(0)-catalyzed, enantioselective CH arylation to
generate macrocyclophanes possessing planar chirality from
simple starting materials has been successfully developed.
Finely tuned bifunctional phosphine-carboxylate ligands
were shown to overcome the mechanistic challenges asso-
ciated with this process, allowing to achieve high enantiose-
lectivities. This DKR-based method displays a broad sub-
strate scope with diverse substitution patterns on different
parts of the cyclophane. Mechanistic investigations indicated
that the initial oxidative addition is reversible while the CH

Abstract: Despite the growing importance of planar chiral macrocyclophanes owing to their unique proper- ties in different areas of chemistry, methods that are effective in controlling their planar chirality are re- stricted to certain molecular scaffolds. Herein, we report the first Pd(0)-catalyzed enantioselective intermolecular C H arylation that induces planar chirality by installing bulky aryl groups through dynamic kinetic resolution (DKR). A computer-assisted approach allowed a fine- tuning of the structure of the employed chiral bifunc- tional phosphine-carboxylate ligands to achieve high enantioselectivities. A range of planar chiral macro- cyclophanes were successfully synthesized from config- urationally labile macrocyclic precursors via C H aryla- tion with various perfluoroarenes. Mechanistic investigations indicated that the reaction proceeds via reversible oxidative addition and enantiodetermining C H activation. Selected macrocyclophane products showed interesting photophysical and chiroptical prop- erties, which depended on both the nature of the ansa chains and the aromatic moieties.
